The agenda today will have a very, I think, really interesting presentation on commercial revitalization murals. Staff's been working for some time on developing the concepts for a murals program for us here in Fairfax County.

It would be a major piece of our placemaking approach to economic development and revitalization of our older communities especially. We're going to have an Investor Entrepreneur Forms Program proposal, and that's going to be presented virtually by Paula Serral, who is the Associate Vice President of Innovation and Economic Development at George Mason University, And it is a follow-up to a board matter that was done very recently, September 12th, asking that this be looked into.

And finally, time permitting, and I think it will permit, but we will see. Board members have been provided a copy of the Local Economic Initiatives Project Status Report. Very interesting, something we will review quickly and give you an opportunity to ask questions about if we have time.

Otherwise, you have the report and you can take a look at it at your leisure. So unless someone has anything, before we get started, I will turn it over to Elizabeth Haag and for the presentation on the Commercial Revitalization Murals Program.

Thank you so much. My name is Elizabeth Haag, and I am the director of the Community Revitalization Section in the Department of Planning and Development. So good morning, Chairman and members of the Board. Today, we are presenting a proposed mural program for the county's commercial revitalization districts and areas for your consideration.

Now, in recent years, community revitalization has been exploring opportunities to use placemaking as a revitalization strategy to foster economic vibrancy in our commercial revitalization districts and areas.

One facet of placemaking is to build on an area's unique assets and history through public art such as murals. Now, the board has previously expressed strong interest in encouraging murals in the community revitalization districts and areas, and so we have developed this proposal for your consideration.

If the board should confirm that this proposal is on target, Our intention would be to come back to the board to seek funding through the Economic Opportunity Reserve Fund. Now, as with any new program, it is expected that as experience is gained, there may be need for refinements.

Thus, we are proposing this program as a pilot initiative for the commercial revitalization districts and areas only. However, as experiences gained and lessons learned, we expect to share what we have learned for possible application in other parts of Fairfax County.
So now I will turn the presentation over to Janae Padmore, who is the Community Revitalization Section's new placemaking planner. Take it away, Janae. Thanks, Liz.

Good morning, Chairman McKay and members of the board. Our proposed program was developed by researching best practices and utilizing my prior experience working with DC Walls. We had in-depth conversations with Arch Fairfax to learn about their knowledge and practices in recruiting and retaining artists.

We have interviewed numerous mural artists regarding their experience and preferred public art processes, and to obtain costs and requirements to develop murals. We have researched previously established mural programs and spoken with their coordinators.

Additionally, we have utilized academic research to develop our approaches. We have also met with each of the supervisors who have a CRD or CRA in their district and have attempted to incorporate their suggested changes to the program.

Murals as a placemaking tool assist in shaping the physical and social character of an area. For the purposes of this program, a mural is defined as a painting or work executed directly onto an exterior surface as accessible to the public without a commercial message.

Murals can be part of a larger strategy to revitalize our older commercial districts in areas that can contribute to the economic competitiveness of these areas. Tools can be used to promote resources and advantages of a locality, celebrate unique local aspects of a community, and create excitement and buzz about a place.

We will be establishing a body to assist in forming recommendations for both the selection of a mural site and the selection of an artist for that site. It will be called the Site and Artist Selection Committee or S.A.S.C.

The S.A.S.C. will have seven members. membership will be comprised of three persons: the Painted Fairfax Murals Program Manager, a representative from Arts Fairfax, and the CRS Section Director. There will be four rotating slots that will be specific to each CRD or CRA. This membership will be comprised of the property owner or the representative, a representative from corresponding supervisor's office, the revitalization program manager for that district, and a revitalization partner

representative. A mural site must first be identified before an artwork can be commissioned. CRS staff will work with community stakeholders to identify potential sites as well as potential aesthetics and themes for these sites. Once a site has been chosen, CRS staff will confirm a property owner's willingness to have a mural on that building, then the SASC for that particular

site will be formed. The SASC will have access to the artist database to identify three potential artists that can fulfill the mural criteria. The identified artist will be sent a call for submission, request that asks each artist to submit a concept to the committee. The submission must incorporate The artist's required community engagement and public education process.

The SASC will select the project artist for the designated exterior surface. The artist will create a draft mural concept for review by the SASC. Zoning Administration will review the proposed mural concept to make a determination that it is not a sign.

The design will be finalized and the SASC will make its final recommendation to the Director of DPD for approval. The mural then can be funded and installed. Finally, we will celebrate the mural's installation. It is essential that murals be seen as a strategy with longevity.

All site owners that agree to a mural will be required to allow the mural to remain for a minimum of five years. This will be codified in a written agreement between the muralist and the county. The program will establish policies to address any damage or vandalism to a mural.

All murals must display the painted Fairfax logo, which is still to be developed. We have researched the cost of various murals of different sizes and with different materials or techniques. To successfully attract artists for a specific site, we'll be paying three artists to submit presentations for the project for a total of $1,500, $500 per artist. The selected artist fee is estimated to range from $6,000 to $35,000,

depending on the size and nature of the project. The fee will include materials, travel, work costs, public education, and mural touch-up for up to five years. A key component of our proposed program is that the community be engaged in the process of developing the mural design.

To maximize our effort, we are budgeting $500 for the development and execution of a robust community engagement process. We are proposing to establish a pilot revitalization murals program with the goal of funding at least two murals per CRD or CRA. For cost estimation purposes, we are assuming one small and one large mural per CRD, which breaks

down to approximately $8,000 to $37,000 depending based on their size. The total cost for two murals in each CRD or CRA is estimated to be $45,000. However, because the Richmond Highway CRD is so much larger than the other CRDs, we are proposing more funds for this area, $85,000. The total for the eight CRDs/CRAs is $400,000. However, we further assume that we can be successful in obtaining approximately 25% of the cost of these murals overall from

grant funding. Thus, the estimated total requirement for this pilot program is $300,000. And with that, we will take any questions you may have. Thank you very much.
